blogs.title: Standing Still: How America First Legal Foundation v. Jamieson Greer Refines Procedural Injury Doctrine
blogs.description: This post breaks down the D.C. Circuit’s application of Article III standing requirements to AFL’s claim of a procedural injury under the Office of Special Counsel’s alleged duty to investigate FOIA violations. It explains why the court found no concrete, particularized harm—citing Summers v. Earth Island Inst., Lujan, and the causation/redressability analysis—and explores what this means for future lawsuits seeking “investigative relief” rather than direct information production.

blogs.title: Mandate or Discretion? Interpreting Section 1216’s ‘Shall Conduct’ Amid Judicial Deference
blogs.description: This entry examines the clash between the statutorily‑mandated language (‘shall conduct an investigation’) in 5 U.S.C. § 1216(a)(3) and the later discretionary clause in § 1216(c). It analyzes how Chevron deference and Heckler v. Chaney inform the court’s conclusion that OSC retains broad discretion, reviews prior cases such as Carson v. Office of Special Counsel, and asks whether any judiciary‑issued mandamus could ever compel an agency action when a statute uses ostensibly mandatory verbs.

blogs.title: Two Paths, One Goal: The Tension Between FOIA’s Built‑in OSC Enforcement (§552) and the Separate Scheme in §§1214–1216
blogs.description: This article maps out Congress’s dual framework for overseeing alleged arbitrary FOIA withholding—the trigger‑based provision in § 552(a)(4)(F)(i) that activates OSC after a court order, and the broader investigative authority granted by §§ 1214–1216 that treats FOIA violations as prohibited personnel practices. It assesses how America First Legal Foundation v. Greer highlights unresolved conflicts in statutory design, surveys prior circuit decisions attempting to harmonize them, and proposes legislative fixes to eliminate ambiguity.

blogs.title: The Diminishing Shield: What This D.C. Circuit Ruling Means for Future FOIA Oversight and Transparency Advocacy
blogs.description: Looking beyond doctrinal minutiae, this piece discusses the practical impact of denying standing against the Office of Special Counsel. It situates the decision within a broader trend of courts tightening procedural‑injury claims by NGOs and partisan groups, evaluates how it may hamper attempts to use OSC as a watchdog over agency transparency policies, and outlines possible policy responses—ranging from congressional amendments clarifying investigatory duties to strategic shifts toward direct district‑court FOIA suits.
